overview: The Göktürk empires joined mobile pastoral power with cities, farms and Silk Road trade across a vast and changing part of Eurasia. The first khaganate split into eastern and western realms; Tang forces defeated the Western Turkic ruler in 657. This atlas still labels a large 700 to 800 outline “Western Gokturk Khaganate,” so the card follows the On Oq legacy, the Türgesh and the Karluk transition rather than pretending one state ruled unchanged for that whole century.

periods.title: One expanding khaganate
periods.summary: The Ashina-led Türk polity expanded rapidly across Inner Asia before eastern and western courts became separate.

periods.title: Eastern and western khaganates
periods.summary: Separate rulers competed and cooperated across enormous distances; Tang armies defeated the western ruler in 657.

periods.title: Claims, local rulers and the On Oq legacy
periods.summary: Tang officials claimed protectorates while western Turkic groups and local principalities continued to contest power.

periods.title: Türgesh rule in the western region
periods.summary: Türgesh rulers adopted the western imperial legacy and governed from centers including Nevaket and Suyab.

periods.title: Karluk succession
periods.summary: Karluks took Suyab in 766. The atlas’s late western outline is therefore a successor landscape, not a surviving Western Turkic state.

sections.title: An empire that kept changing shape

items.text: The name Türk first appears as the ruling name of the sixth-century khaganate, but “the Göktürks” did not remain one government. Rival courts, family branches and allied groups made eastern and western histories diverge. A colored polygon is especially misleading here: it cannot show seasonal movement, layered loyalties or a distant ruler’s uneven reach.

Tang armies defeated the Western Turkic ruler Ashina Helu in 657 and claimed authority through protectorates. Those claims met resistance, Tibetan expansion and strong local rulers. A court could appear on an imperial map without every field, market and mountain pass being administered day by day from China.

Around 699 the Türgesh leader Wuzhile established power from the Tashkent region toward Dzungaria, using headquarters at Nevaket and the Ili. His successors fought Tang-backed rivals and Arab armies. They inherited western Turkic titles and political traditions, but historians describe a new Türgesh state rather than an unbroken Western Turkic khaganate.

The eastern Second Turkic Khaganate fell in the 740s, while events in the west followed a different path. Karluks moved into On Oq territory and took Suyab in 766. Putting both endings in one card prevents a tidy but false story in which every Türk realm ended on the same day.

sections.title: Towns, tents and a very busy road

items.text: The Chuy valley contained walled centers such as Suyab and Navikat. Archaeology and written sources point to merchants, farmers and warriors living in and around these settlements. Pastoral groups and farming towns depended on one another for animals, grain, transport, craft goods and access to routes across the mountains.

The wider Silk Roads corridor preserved canals, pipes and reservoirs that supported farming and towns in Zhetysu. That is firm evidence for organized water work. It is not evidence that every household had a flushing toilet, so the honest bathroom answer is: water engineering, yes; a universal toilet system, not demonstrated by these sources.

Sogdian merchants traveled far beyond their home cities. Under Turkic protection, envoys reached Byzantium in 568 to seek a silk market that bypassed Sasanian control. Long-distance trade depended on interpreters, credit, pack animals and political negotiation; a caravan was closer to a moving business network than a line of camels following a road sign.

Trade also left words behind. Old Turkic borrowed commercial vocabulary from Sogdian, including terms connected with debt and coins. Language traveled with contracts and conversations as surely as silk did. Borrowing a useful word was not a loss of identity; it was proof that people were doing business face to face.

Türk and Sogdian elites formed marriage alliances, and art from the region combines clothing, symbols and visual habits associated with both communities. Elite marriages do not describe every family, but they show that diplomacy could happen around a wedding as well as across a battlefield.

One Chinese account says Sogdian boys began learning books around age five and were then taught commerce. It is a valuable outsider’s glimpse of literacy and family training among trading communities, not a school-enrollment statistic and not a rule for every child. Girls’ education is not described clearly enough in this checked evidence to invent an answer.

Buddhist temples, a Zoroastrian fire altar and cemetery, and stones with Christian inscriptions have all been reported in the Chuy valley. People with different beliefs met in the same connected region. A traveler could encounter more kinds of worship than lunch, and lunch was probably complicated enough.

The checked evidence does not establish a single Göktürk medical system, public hospital network or standard household toilet. Waterworks, food production and religious institutions certainly affected health, but they do not justify invented doctors or bathroom fixtures. Sometimes the funniest reliable fact is that archaeology has not yet found the royal plumbing manual.

Western Turkic and Türgesh rulers issued bronze coins with square holes, adapting a familiar cash-coin form while adding Sogdian writing and Turkic titles. Some pieces also carry tamgas, compact dynastic signs. The hole made strings of coins easier to handle; it did not make the coin itself square, despite trying very hard.

A Türgesh coin legend has been published as βγy twrkys’ γ’γ’n pny, read approximately “coin of the divine/lord Türgesh qaghan.” This is a scholarly transliteration of Sogdian letters seen on coins, not a facsimile of the ancient shapes. It is a compact written witness to a Turkic ruler using Sogdian for public authority.

Sogdian served more than merchants: it appeared in early Turkic administration and monumental writing. The late sixth-century Bugut inscription is an important example of a Turkic imperial text written in Sogdian. Later Old Turkic runiform inscriptions belonged especially to the eastern Second Khaganate, so the two writing traditions should not be collapsed into one alphabet.

Excavation at Suyab has uncovered Buddhist sanctuaries, a Zoroastrian cemetery and Christian remains alongside urban defenses and workshops. The city became a Black Türgesh capital in 738, was attacked in 748 and passed to Karluk control in the 760s. A city could change rulers repeatedly while its streets and communities outlasted a dynasty.

ending.text: There was no single Göktürk ending. Tang forces defeated the western khagan in 657; the Türgesh later rebuilt steppe power in much of the western region; Karluks took Suyab in 766. The eastern Second Turkic Khaganate fell in the 740s. Türk-speaking communities, cities and political traditions continued, and later states reused titles, routes and institutions. The atlas’s 800 edge is a map cutoff, not the disappearance of a people.
